channel.title: Oddly Wired
channel.description: One checked psychology fact a day. Every claim names the study behind it.

item.title: You overestimate how much you will change in the future.
item.description: In a 2013 survey, people recognized how much they changed in the past but insisted their current personality was set for the future.

item.title: You feel an urge to act because you were asked.
item.description: Researchers found that simply being asked for a small favor increased a participant's future liking for that person.

item.title: You underestimate how much others appreciate your kindness.
item.description: People consistently expect their expressions of gratitude to be less impactful than they actually are to the recipient.

item.title: You value things more just because you made them.
item.description: People rate items they partially assembled as equal in value to items built by professionals.

item.title: You judge people by their actions but yourself by your intentions.
item.description: Although Jones and Nisbett (1971) proposed that people attribute their own actions to situational factors while attributing others' to dispositional factors, subsequent research, including a 2006 meta-analysis, suggests this asymmetry is not as consistent or widespread as once thought.

item.title: You are blind to the persistence of your own thoughts.
item.description: The harder you attempt to suppress a specific thought, the more frequently it enters your awareness.

item.title: You adjust your identity to match your recent decisions.
item.description: After making a difficult choice, you will inflate the value of your chosen option and devalue the rejected one.

item.title: You find people more attractive if they show flaws.
item.description: Highly competent individuals are often rated more favorably after making a minor, relatable blunder, while less competent individuals are typically rated less favorably.

item.title: You interpret physical warmth as personal social acceptance.
item.description: A 2008 study reported that holding a hot beverage could lead to warmer social evaluations, but this effect has failed to replicate in subsequent research.

item.title: You assign human traits to objects to satisfy a need for connection.
item.description: A 2008 study found that individuals experiencing social exclusion were more likely to attribute human-like intentions to inanimate gadgets.

item.title: You learn faster when you expect to teach the material.
item.description: A 2014 study found that participants who prepared to teach information performed significantly better on recall tests than those who prepared to be tested themselves.

item.title: You are more creative when your physical environment feels expansive.
item.description: A 2007 study by Meyers-Levy and Zhu in the Journal of Consumer Research showed that ceiling height influences whether individuals engage in abstract, relational thinking or concrete, detail-oriented thinking.

item.title: You are more likely to reach goals you write down by hand.
item.description: A 2014 study suggested that handwriting may promote deeper processing of information than typing, though subsequent attempts to replicate these findings have yielded inconsistent results.

item.title: Your hands are not just reflecting your thoughts; they are thinking.
item.description: A 2009 study showed that students who were encouraged to gesture while explaining math problems retained the information better than those told to keep their hands still.

item.title: Nostalgia actually makes you feel physically warmer.
item.description: A 2012 study found that participants induced to feel nostalgic reported significantly higher perceived ambient temperatures.

item.title: You remember less of the event you photograph.
item.description: In a 2014 study, participants who took photos of objects in a museum remembered fewer details about those objects than those who simply observed them.

item.title: You value things more once you possess them.
item.description: The mere ownership effect is the finding that items are rated as more attractive simply because they are labeled as belonging to you.

item.title: You assume everyone is watching your every move.
item.description: The spotlight effect is the tendency to overestimate how much others notice your appearance or your behavior.

item.title: You underestimate the power of your own habits.
item.description: Automaticity is the ability of well-practiced behaviors to run without conscious supervision or intent.

item.title: You are influenced by the first thing you hear.
item.description: The primacy effect in conversation means the first piece of information you receive about a person disproportionately shapes your entire impression.

item.title: Wait times seem longer when you are uncertain.
item.description: The uncertainty effect in waiting demonstrates that people perceive wait times as significantly longer when the end of the wait is unknown.

item.title: You struggle to accept information that changes your mind.
item.description: Motivated skepticism is the tendency to scrutinize counter-attitudinal information more intensely than information that supports your existing views.

item.title: Groups make riskier decisions than individuals alone.
item.description: Group polarization describes the finding that group discussion often leads members to advocate for more extreme positions than they held individually; risky shift is a specific subset of this phenomenon where the extreme position is specifically the riskier one.

item.title: You are worse at predicting your own behavior.
item.description: The introspection illusion is the tendency to trust one's own introspections as a reliable source of information while failing to recognize that cognitive biases operate unconsciously.

item.title: Events do not make you as happy as expected.
item.description: The hedonic treadmill, a concept proposed by Brickman and Campbell in 1971, hypothesizes a tendency to return to a baseline happiness level, though modern psychological research suggests this adaptation is not universal.

item.title: You judge an explanation as 'correct' if it includes neuroscience data.
item.description: The seductive allure of neuroscience makes people believe that explanations are logically sound, even when they contain completely irrelevant brain science.

item.title: Shared suffering increases cooperation more than shared rewards do.
item.description: Groups that endure an unpleasant experience together develop stronger bonds than groups that experience a neutral activity together.

item.title: Holding a warm drink makes you perceive people as kinder.
item.description: An initial 2008 study suggested that physical warmth might prime interpersonal warmth, though subsequent larger-scale replication attempts have failed to confirm this effect.

item.title: Moderate background noise actually improves your creative thinking performance.
item.description: A 2012 study found that 70 decibels of ambient noise enhances performance on creative tasks, while 85 decibels proves too distracting.

item.title: You remember words significantly better if you read them aloud.
item.description: The production effect shows that articulating information improves memory compared to reading it silently.

item.title: You reach goals faster when you create an if-then plan.
item.description: Formulating 'if-then' statements increases the likelihood of goal attainment because it delegates control to the environment.

item.title: You feel less distressed just by naming your emotions.
item.description: Affect labeling—putting your feelings into words—significantly reduces activity in the amygdala, the brain's emotional center.

item.title: You value things more once you claim them.
item.description: A 1990 study showed that people value an object significantly more simply because they consider it to be 'theirs' for a short period.

item.title: Your brain creates patterns where there are none.
item.description: A 2008 study found that individuals who were prompted to feel a lack of control were more likely to perceive illusory patterns in random noise.

item.title: You fear social exclusion more than you admit.
item.description: A 2003 study indicated that even brief experiences of social rejection trigger activity in the brain's dorsal anterior cingulate cortex.

item.title: You view your own moral failures as situational accidents.
item.description: A 1971 study by Jones and Nisbett proposed that actors attribute their own behaviors to situational factors while observers attribute the same behaviors to stable dispositions.

item.title: You interpret your own past as more stable than it was.
item.description: In a 2000 study, individuals retrospectively adjusted their past attitudes to align with their current beliefs, falsely remembering their younger selves as holding their modern opinions.

item.title: Your brain hides its lack of preparation from you.
item.description: A 2002 study showed that people believe they have a deeper understanding of complex mechanical devices than they actually possess.

item.title: You claim to understand concepts that do not exist.
item.description: In a 2003 study, participants consistently claimed knowledge of nonexistent academic terms when asked to rate their familiarity with various topics.

item.title: You make decisions based on the first thing you hear.
item.description: A 1974 experiment showed that asking participants if the population of a city was greater than 5 million or 200 thousand radically skewed their final estimates.

item.title: Your brain creates a story to explain your physical reactions.
item.description: In a 1962 experiment, subjects were injected with adrenaline and told it was a vitamin, leading them to misinterpret their jittery nerves as happiness or anger depending on the social setting.

item.title: Your eye movements reflect your internal search patterns.
item.description: Visual search time increases linearly with set size specifically during serial (conjunction) search, whereas feature search is conducted in parallel with a near-zero slope.

item.title: You repeat a story until the details disappear.
item.description: A classic study showed that when participants retold a story over several sessions, they consistently simplified the narrative and discarded unconventional details.

item.title: Time perception changes as you get older.
item.description: Research indicates that your sense of how fast time passes is linked to how much new information you encode; as encoding slows, time feels like it accelerates.

item.title: You subconsciously shift your persona for every setting.
item.description: Individuals who score high in self-monitoring intentionally adjust their behavior to match the expectations of their immediate social environment.

item.title: Curiosity is the physical feeling of a missing piece.
item.description: A 1994 analysis defined curiosity as a 'cognitively induced deprivation' triggered by the awareness of a gap in one's knowledge.

item.title: Remembering to remember is a distinct, fragile process.
item.description: Research shows that prospective memory—the ability to perform a future intention—relies on different brain mechanisms than retrospective memory.

item.title: Your language shapes how your brain perceives color.
item.description: A 2007 study showed that Russian speakers, who have distinct words for light and dark blue, could categorize these colors faster than English speakers.

item.title: High visual focus can render you temporarily deaf.
item.description: A 2011 study found that participants focused on a difficult visual task failed to hear a distinct tone played repeatedly in their ears.

item.title: Describing a face makes you worse at identifying it.
item.description: A 1990 study found that participants who wrote a verbal description of a face were significantly less likely to correctly pick it out of a lineup later.
